Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 47, verses 4–9:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿So when you meet those who disbelieve, [smite] the necks until, when you have inflicted slaughter upon them, then bind fast the bonds; and afterward either [free them as] a favor or ransom [them] until the war lays down its burdens. That [is the command]. And had Allah willed, He could have taken vengeance upon them [Himself], but [He ordered war] to test some of you by means of others. And those who are killed in the cause of Allah — He will never allow their deeds to be lost.﴾ ﴿He will guide them and amend their condition.﴾ ﴿And admit them to Paradise, which He has made known to them.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, if you support Allah, He will support you and plant firmly your feet.﴾ ﴿But those who disbelieve — for them is destruction, and He will waste their deeds.﴾ ﴿That is because they hated what Allah revealed, so He has rendered worthless their deeds.﴾

Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, Ibn Jurayj, al-Suddi and al-Dahhak said: this verse is abrogated (mansukh) by the verse of the sword in Bara'ah: ﴿Then kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5], and that taking captives, granting favor and accepting ransom have been lifted. Thus, whenever a captive is taken, killing necessarily accompanies it. A similar view is narrated from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him. Ibn 'Umar and 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, may Allah be pleased with them, and 'Ata' said, in substance: this verse is muhkam (definitive), clarifying that other verse, and granting favor and ransom are established. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ granted favor to Thumamah ibn Uthal and ransomed the captives of Badr. Al-Hasan also said this, and said: a captive is killed only in war, in order to instill awe in the enemy. 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, may Allah be pleased with him, would ransom one man for another, while al-Hasan prohibited ransoming with wealth. 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz ordered the killing of a captive from the Turks who was reported to him to have killed Muslims. A group said: this verse was specified by the other verse only with regard to the People of the Book; for them there is favor and ransom, while idol-worshippers face nothing but killing.

According to the view of most scholars, the two verses are both muhkam. His saying here, ﴿smite the necks﴾, is equivalent to His saying there: ﴿Then kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5]. Here He explicitly mentions favor and ransom, which He did not explicitly mention there, and this is a matter already established. This is the strong opinion.

His saying ﴿smite the necks﴾ (ḍarb al-riqab) is a verbal noun (maṣdar) in the sense of the verb, meaning: strike their necks. He specified the most well-known and recognized type of killing and mentioned it, while the intended meaning is: kill them in whatever manner is possible. Another verse adds: ﴿and strike every fingertip of them﴾ [al-Anfal: 12], and this is among the most painful blows of war, because it disables the whole body of the one struck, since the fingertip is the greatest and most fundamental instrument of the fighter. ﴿Athkhantumuhum﴾ means: by killing. "Al-ithkhan" among a people means that killed and wounded become numerous among them. The meaning is: then bind fast the bonds on those who were not killed and upon whom nothing but capture has been imposed. "Mannan" and "fida'an" are two verbal nouns in the accusative, governed by two implied verbs. The majority of reciters read "fida'an," while Shibl, from Ibn Kathir, read "fada," with a short vowel (maqsuran).

The leader of the Muslims has discretion regarding his captives in five ways: killing, enslavement, imposing the jizyah, or ransom. The consideration is weighed according to the captive's condition, whether he harms the Muslims or the opposite.

His saying ﴿until the war lays down its burdens﴾ means: until its weights and instruments depart and cease. "Al-awzar" is the plural of wizr, the loads carried in it and the implements for it. From this is the saying of 'Amr ibn Ma'd Yakrib al-Zubaydi:

"I prepared for war its burdens: long spears and male horses."

Al-Tha'labi said: It was also said that "al-awzar" in this verse means sins, the plural of wizr, because war must inevitably involve sins on one of the two sides.

The interpreters differed about the point at which the war lays down its burdens. Qatadah said: until all submit, and then the war lays down its burdens. The shrewd scholars of reflection said: until you overcome them and kill them. Mujahid said: until 'Isa ibn Maryam, peace be upon them both, descends.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The apparent meaning of the verse is that it is a metaphor intended to indicate the perpetual continuation of the command, since war between believers and disbelievers never lays down its burdens. This is like saying: "I will do such-and-such until the Day of Resurrection," meaning that you will do it constantly.

His saying ﴿That [is the command]﴾ — its implied meaning is: the matter is that. Then His saying ﴿And had Allah willed, He could have taken vengeance upon them﴾ means: by a punishment from Him by which He would destroy them in a single moment. But He willed to test the believers, and to try some people by means of others. The majority of reciters read "qatalu," while 'Asim, al-Ju'dari (in one narration from him) read "qataluu" with fatha on the qaf and ta'. Abu 'Amr, Hafs from 'Asim, al-A'raj, Qatadah and al-A'mash read "qutilu" with damma on the qaf and kasra on the ta'. Zayd ibn Thabit, al-Hasan, al-Ju'dari, 'Isa and Abu Raja' read it likewise but with a shaddah on the ta'. The first reading is more general and clearer in meaning.

Qatadah said: this verse was revealed concerning those who were killed on the Day of Uhud. His saying ﴿sayahdihim﴾ means: to the path of Paradise. The discussion of "amending their condition" has already been mentioned. 'Abbas ibn al-Mufaddal narrated from Abu 'Amr: "wa yudkhilhum" with a sukun on the lam; and in al-Taghabun, ﴿on the Day He gathers you﴾ [al-Taghabun: 9], and in Surat al-Insan, ﴿We feed you only﴾ [al-Insan: 9], with a sukun on the ta' and the mim.

His saying ﴿'arrafaha lahum﴾: Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, Qatadah and Mujahid said: its meaning is: He made it clear to them, meaning He made them know their dwellings in it. In a similar sense is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "One of you is more knowing of his dwelling in Paradise than of his dwelling in this world." A group said: its meaning is: He named it for them and marked it, each dwelling by the name of its owner; this is a kind of "ta'rif." Another group said: its meaning is: He honored it for them, raised it and elevated it; this is from the a'raf, which are the mountains and the like, and from it come the "a'raf" of horses. Mu'arrij and others said: its meaning is: He perfumed it, derived from "al-'urf," and from it comes "ta'am mu'arraf," meaning seasoned, and 'arafa al-qidr means I seasoned the pot with salt and spices.

His saying ﴿in tansuru Allah﴾ contains an elision of a noun, meaning: the religion of Allah and His Messenger. The meaning is: if you support Him with your earnestness, your following and your faith, He will support you by creating strength and courage in you and other such knowledge. The majority of reciters read "wa yuthabbit" with a fatha on the mutharrathah ta' and a shaddah on the ba'; al-Mufaddal from 'Asim read "wa yuthbit" with a sukun on the tha' and a lightened ba'. This firming is in the places of battle for Islam, and it was also said: on the Sirat on the Day of Resurrection.

His saying ﴿fata'san lahum﴾ means: stumbling and destruction for them. It is a word said against the disbeliever, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"O my master, if I stumble, take me by the hand, and do not say: 'No,' nor say: 'Ta'isan.'"

al-A'sha said on this meaning:

"With a she-camel that twists her neck when she stumbles, so ta's is nearer to her than my saying: 'La'a.'"

From it is the saying of the mother of Mistah when she stumbled in her cloak: "Ta'isa Mistah." Ibn al-Sikkit said: al-ta'su is to fall on one's face. "Ta'san" is a verbal noun governed by an implied verb.

His saying ﴿karihu ma anzala Allah﴾ means the Qur'an. His saying ﴿fa-ahbata a'malahum﴾ implies that their deeds in their disbelief, which are righteous, are bound and preserved. There is no disagreement that the disbeliever has guardians who record his evil deeds. People differed about his good deeds. One group said: they are nullified, and they are rewarded for them only with the blessings of this world. Another group said: they are counted for the reward of this world, and because the [disbeliever] may later embrace Islam, those deeds are added to his good deeds in Islam. This is one of the two interpretations of the saying of the Prophet ﷺ to Hakim ibn Hizam: "You have embraced Islam upon whatever good you had previously done." Some said: its meaning is: you embraced Islam on condition that what good preceded you be counted for you; this is the interpretation we pointed to. Another group said: its meaning is: you embraced Islam with the dropping of what good preceded you, since you have already been rewarded for it with the blessings of your worldly life. Al-Tabari mentioned that the deeds which the verse reports as being nullified are their worship of idols and their disbelief. The meaning of "uhbita" is: He made them into deeds that do not grow and are not regarded as valid, so they are, for that reason, like what has been nullified.

His saying ﴿fata'san lahum﴾ means: stumbling and destruction for them. It is a word said against the disbeliever, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"O my master, if I stumble, take me by the hand, and do not say: 'No,' nor say: 'Ta'isan.'"

al-A'sha said on this meaning:

"With a she-camel that twists her neck when she stumbles, so ta's is nearer to her than my saying: 'La'a.'"

From it is the saying of the mother of Mistah when she stumbled in her cloak: "Ta'isa Mistah." Ibn al-Sikkit said: al-ta'su is to fall on one's face. "Ta'san" is a verbal noun governed by an implied verb.

Another group said: they are counted for the reward of this world, and because the [disbeliever] may later embrace Islam, those deeds are added to his good deeds in Islam. Ibn 'Umar and 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, may Allah be pleased with them, and 'Ata' said, in substance: this verse is muhkam (definitive), clarifying that other verse, and granting favor and ransom are established. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ granted favor to Thumamah ibn Uthal and ransomed the captives of Badr. Al-Hasan also said this, and said: a captive is killed only in war, in order to instill awe in the enemy. 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, may Allah be pleased with him, would ransom one man for another, while al-Hasan prohibited ransoming with wealth. 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz ordered the killing of a captive from the Turks who was reported to him to have killed Muslims. A group said: this verse was specified by the other verse only with regard to the People of the Book; for them there is favor and ransom, while idol-worshippers face nothing but killing.

Here He explicitly mentions favor and ransom, which He did not explicitly mention there, and this is a matter already established. This is the strong opinion.

Another verse adds: ﴿and strike every fingertip of them﴾ [al-Anfal: 12], and this is among the most painful blows of war, because it disables the whole body of the one struck, since the fingertip is the greatest and most fundamental instrument of the fighter. ﴿Athkhantumuhum﴾ means: by killing. The meaning is: then bind fast the bonds on those who were not killed and upon whom nothing but capture has been imposed. The majority of reciters read "fida'an," while Shibl, from Ibn Kathir, read "fada," with a short vowel (maqsuran).

The leader of the Muslims has discretion regarding his captives in five ways: killing, enslavement, imposing the jizyah, or ransom. The consideration is weighed according to the captive's condition, whether he harms the Muslims or the opposite.

Al-Tha'labi said: It was also said that "al-awzar" in this verse means sins, the plural of wizr, because war must inevitably involve sins on one of the two sides.

The shrewd scholars of reflection said: until you overcome them and kill them. Mujahid said: until 'Isa ibn Maryam, peace be upon them both, descends.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The apparent meaning of the verse is that it is a metaphor intended to indicate the perpetual continuation of the command, since war between believers and disbelievers never lays down its burdens. This is like saying: "I will do such-and-such until the Day of Resurrection," meaning that you will do it constantly.

His saying ﴿That [is the command]﴾ — its implied meaning is: the matter is that. Then His saying ﴿And had Allah willed, He could have taken vengeance upon them﴾ means: by a punishment from Him by which He would destroy them in a single moment. But He willed to test the believers, and to try some people by means of others. The majority of reciters read "qatalu," while 'Asim, al-Ju'dari (in one narration from him) read "qataluu" with fatha on the qaf and ta'. Abu 'Amr, Hafs from 'Asim, al-A'raj, Qatadah and al-A'mash read "qutilu" with damma on the qaf and kasra on the ta'. Zayd ibn Thabit, al-Hasan, al-Ju'dari, 'Isa and Abu Raja' read it likewise but with a shaddah on the ta'. The first reading is more general and clearer in meaning.

﴿Have they not travelled through the land and observed how was the end of those before them? God destroyed them, and for the disbelievers there are similar ones.﴾ ﴿That is because God is the Protector of those who believe, and because the disbelievers have no protector.﴾ ﴿Indeed, God will admit those who believe and do righteous deeds into gardens beneath which rivers flow. But those who disbelieve enjoy themselves and eat as cattle eat, and the Fire is their abode.﴾ ﴿And how many a town, mightier in strength than your town which has driven you out, have We destroyed, and they had no helper.﴾

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Have they not travelled﴾ is a questioning (tawqif) and a rebuke (tawbikh) addressed to the Quraysh. ﴿Those before them﴾ refers to Thamud, the people of Lot, the people of Shu'ayb, the people of the Barrier (al-Sadd), and others. "Ad-dammar" (destruction) means corruption, the demolition of buildings, and the removal of habitation. His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿God destroyed them﴾ is derived from this meaning. The pronoun in His saying ﴿"similar ones"﴾ may refer to the outcome mentioned, and it may also validly refer to the act implied in His saying ﴿God destroyed them﴾.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That is because﴾ is an introductory statement, and the clause introduced by "anna" (that) is its predicate. This verse was revealed on the day of Uhud, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) derived from it his response to Abu Sufyan when he said to him: "God is our Protector, and you have no protector."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and eat as cattle eat﴾ means eating devoid of thought and reflection. The comparison occurs only in what goes beyond eating, namely in their scant thinking and lack of reflection. Thus His saying, "as" (kama), is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal). This is like when you say: "The ignorant man lives the life of a beast." Literally, the ignorant, the knowledgeable, and the beast are equal in that each has a life; but the meaning of your statement is: he lives devoid of reflection and understanding, just as the beast lives.

"Al-mathwa" means the place of residence. The discussion of His saying, ﴿"and how many"﴾, has already been presented more than once. God, exalted is He, set forth for Makkah an example from the towns that were destroyed despite their greatness, such as the town of the people of 'Ad and others. ﴿"Expelled you"﴾ means the time of the Hijrah (emigration). He attributed the expulsion to the town, taking the wording (lafz) into account, and He said ﴿"We destroyed them"﴾, taking the meaning (ma'na) into account. It is said that this verse was revealed right after the Prophet (ﷺ) left Makkah on the road to Madinah. It is also said that it was revealed in Madinah, and it is said that it was revealed in Makkah after Hudaybiyyah, in the year he entered it, the Messenger of God (ﷺ). It is also said that it was revealed in the year of the Conquest while he was approaching it. All of this has the ruling of a Madinan verse.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 47, verses 14–16:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿Is one who is upon clear proof from his Lord like one for whom the evil of his deeds has been made attractive, and who follow their own desires?﴾ ﴿The description of Paradise which the God-fearing have been promised: in it are rivers of water unaltered, and rivers of milk whose taste does not change, and rivers of wine, a delight to those who drink, and rivers of purified honey. For them therein is every kind of fruit, and forgiveness from their Lord. Is it like one who abides forever in the Fire and is given boiling water to drink, which cuts through their bowels?﴾ ﴿And among them are those who listen to you, until, when they leave your presence, they say to those who were given knowledge, "What did he just say?" Those are the ones upon whose hearts God has set a seal, and who follow their own desires.﴾

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Is one who is﴾, the verse. It is a reproach and an affirmation concerning a matter on which there is agreement, and it sets up an equation between these two groups. Qatadah said: the reference of this verse is to Muhammad (ﷺ) in that he is the one upon clear proof from his Lord, and to the disbelievers of Quraysh in that they are the ones for whom the evil of their deeds has been made attractive. The wording remains general for the people of these two attributes until the end of time. His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿upon clear proof from his Lord﴾ means: upon a clear matter, a bright and manifest creed. It is possible that the meaning is "upon a clear affair and a clear religion," and the ha' (of bayyinah) has been added for emphasis, as in 'allamah and nassabah. The one to whom His saying ﴿"zuyyina" (was made attractive)﴾ is attributed is Satan. And "following desires" means obeying them, as though they proceed in one direction and the person proceeds along with them.

People differed concerning the meaning of His saying ﴿The description (mathal) of Paradise﴾, the verse. al-Nadr ibn Shumayl and others said: "mathal" means "ṣifah" (description, attribute). It is as though He said: the description of Paradise is what you hear about it, that in it is such and such. Sibawayh said: the meaning is: "in what is recited to you, the description of Paradise," then He explained what is recited by His saying: "in it is such and such." What led some to make "mathal" equivalent to "ṣifah" is that the thing compared to is not present in the verse. It appears that the intention in the comparison is to the thing that a person imagines upon hearing "in it is such and such," for he then conceives of gardens in this form, and that is the likeness (mathal) and example (mithal) of Paradise. Or there is an ellipsis in the speech required by the apparent sense, as though He, the Exalted, says: the likeness of Paradise is manifest in the mind of whoever comprehends these attributes. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, read "mithal al-jannah" (the example of Paradise), and 'Ali ibn Abi Talib also, and Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him, read "amthal al-jannah" (the examples of Paradise). According to all these interpretations, in His saying ﴿like one who abides forever﴾ there is an ellipsis whose estimate is: "Are those who dwell in this (Paradise)?" or whose estimate is: "Are these people?" as a reference to the God-fearing. It is also possible in my view that the ellipsis is at the beginning of the verse, as though He, the Exalted, said: "Is the likeness of the people of Paradise like one who abides forever in the Fire?" and His saying would then be interrogative without the interrogative alif. The meaning is: "Is the likeness of the people of Paradise, who have these attributes, like one who abides forever in the Fire?" (p-648) His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance and grants them their taqwa (God-consciousness).﴾ ﴿Do they then await anything but the Hour, that it should come upon them suddenly? Its signs have already come. And Allah knows your moving about and your resting place.﴾

When the Exalted mentioned the hypocrites with what they deserve, in His saying: ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah has sealed upon their hearts and who followed their desires﴾ [Muhammad: 16], He followed that with mention of the believers, thereby showing the distinction, and He honored them by attributing the act of being guided to them, which is an indication of their earning it. His saying: ﴿He increases them in guidance﴾ may mean that the agent in "zādahum" is Allah the Exalted. The increase in this sense is either by an increase in understanding and proofs, or by the arrival of the legislation, the prohibitions and the reports, so that guidance increases in order that they may increase in knowledge of all of that and in belief in it, and that is by the grace of Allah the Exalted. It may also be that the agent in "zādahum" is the speech of the hypocrites and their turmoil, because that is something at which the believer marvels, praises Allah for his faith, and grows in insight into his religion. So it is as if He, the Exalted, said: "And the guided believers, the act of these hypocrites increased them in guidance," meaning the increase came because of it, so He attributed the act to it. His saying, according to this view, "those who are guided" (ihtadaw) means: in their belief in 'Isa, upon him be peace; then Muhammad ﷺ increased them in guidance when they believed in him. As for the agent in "ātāhum," the statement varies according to the interpretations mentioned, and the strongest of them is that the agent is Allah the Exalted, and "ātāhum" means "gave them," that is, He made them God-conscious toward Him. The sense is: their taqwa of Him. al-A'mash read "wa-anṭāhum," which has the same meaning as "ā'ṭāhum" (gave them); it was related by Muhammad ibn Talha from his father, and it is in the Codex of 'Abdullah.

That is, this is the reality of the matter in itself, even though they themselves are waiting for something other than that, for what is in their souls is not regarded, since it is false. The majority of reciters read "an ta'tiyahum," so "an" is a substitute (badal) for "al-sā'ah" (the Hour). In this reading, His saying: ﴿Its signs have already come﴾ is a new statement, and the fa' is conjoining one sentence to another sentence. The people of Mecca, as transmitted by al-Ru'asi, read "in ta'tihim" with a kasra on the alif and the verb in the jussive on the condition, and the fa' in "fa-qad" is the answer of the condition; it is not conjunctive on the first reading, since there is a kind of conditional meaning in it. His saying: ﴿Its signs have already come﴾, on both readings, means: it is fitting that preparation and fear of it should occur for whoever is certain and takes care of his own soul. What has come of the signs of the Hour is Muhammad, upon him be prayers and peace, since he is the last of the prophets, so a measure of the matter of the Hour has become manifest. In a hadith: that he, upon him be prayers and peace, said: "I am among the signs of the Hour." And he, upon him be prayers and peace, said: "I was sent, and the Hour, like these two," and he indicated with his two fingers, "like two horses in a race." It is said: "sharṭ" or "ashrāṭ," with the ra' unvowelled and lightened. "Ashraṭa al-rajulu nafsahu" means he bound himself to matters. Aws ibn Hajar said:

This is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, and every individual of the community is included in it. Al-Bukhari, may Allah the Exalted have mercy on him, titled a chapter: "Knowledge before speech and action," because of the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Know, then, that there is no god but Allah﴾, and ﴿and ask forgiveness for your sin﴾ (the verse). It is obligatory upon every believer to ask forgiveness for the believing men and believing women. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "Your moving about" is your activity in your worldly life, and "your resting place" is your revival in your graves and in your Hereafter.

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

This is the beginning of a description of the state of the believers in their earnestness in the religion of Allah the Exalted and their eagerness for its triumph, and of the state of the hypocrites, marked by laziness, cowardice, and eagerness for the corruption of the religion and its people. The reason is that the believers' zeal drove them to desire victory, to desire fighting the enemy, and to desire the exposure of the hypocrites, and similar things which are a manifestation of Islam. So they took comfort in revelation and felt lonely when it was delayed, while Allah the Exalted had set that at appointed periods and times that are not exceeded. Thus Allah praised the believers for their eagerness. Their saying, ﴿Why has a surah not been sent down?﴾ means: let it include our manifestation and our command to strive against the enemy and the like.

Qatadah said: every surah in which fighting is mentioned is muhkamah, and it is the most severe of the Qur'an upon the hypocrites. This is a matter Qatadah derived by inference from the Qur'an, and it is not at all part of the tafsir of this verse. In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, it reads: "a surah muhaddathah (newly revealed)". "The disease that is in the hearts" is a metaphor for corruption of belief. The reality of health and sickness is in bodies, and they are borrowed for meanings. The look of the fearful and bewildered person is close to the look of one who has swooned, and their fear is a description and a comparison.

As for His saying, ﴿So woe to them﴾ and the verse: "awla" is of the form af'al, from "walaka al-shay'u yalika" (a thing is near/befalls you). One group said its form is af'ala, and there is inversion (qalb) in it, because it is derived from al-wayl (woe). The well-known usage of "awla" is that you say: "this is awla bika than this" meaning: more deserving. It may also be used as "awla laka" alone, by way of omission and abbreviation of the speech that accompanies it, so you say, in a tone of rebuke and threat: "Awla laka, O so-and-so." And from it is the saying of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, to al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with him: "Awla laka." Another group of exegetes said: "awla" is in the nominative by being the subject (mubtada'), and "ta'ah" is its predicate.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is the well-known usage of "awla." Another group of exegetes said: "awla lahum" is a subject and predicate, meaning rebuke and threat. Then this group differed concerning the meaning of His saying, ﴿obedience and fair speech﴾. Some of them said: the estimate is: obedience and fair speech is more fitting. This is the interpretation of Mujahid and the view of al-Khalil and Sibawayh, and beginning with an indefinite noun is good because it is specified, so it contains some definiteness. Others said: the estimate is: the matter is obedience and fair speech, i.e., the matter pleasing to Allah the Exalted. Others said: the estimate is: their saying to you, O Muhammad, by way of mockery and deception: "obedience and fair speech." Then when the matter is resolved upon, they dislike it. Ka'b al-Ahbar and Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: the meaning is: if you take charge of the affairs of people, from wilayah (authority). On this basis it was said that it was revealed concerning the Banu Hashim and the Banu Umayyah; al-Tha'labi mentioned it. His saying, ﴿Those are the ones whom Allah has cursed﴾ refers to the aforementioned people with diseased hearts. "La'anahum" means He removed them far away. His saying, ﴿so He has deafened them and blinded their eyes﴾ is a metaphor for their not hearing, so it is as if they were blind and deaf.

The words of the Exalted:

﴿Will they not reflect upon the Qur'an, or are there locks upon their hearts?﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who turned back on their heels after guidance had become clear to them—Satan has enticed them and prolonged their hopes.﴾ ﴿That is because they said to those who hated what Allah had revealed, "We will obey you in part of the matter." His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Will they not reflect upon the Qur'an﴾ is a rebuke and a reproach. Reflecting upon the Qur'an is a guarantor of clarification and guidance. The word ﴿أم﴾ (ʾam, "or") here is disjunctive (munqaṭiʿah, i.e., it begins a new question), and it is to be understood as containing the meaning of ﴿بل﴾ (bal, "rather") together with the interrogative alif. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿or are there locks upon their hearts?﴾ is a metaphor (istiʿārah) for the rust (rayn) that their hearts have acquired, which prevented them from faith.

It is related that a delegation from Yemen came to the Prophet (ﷺ), and among them was a young man. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited this verse, and the young man said: "Upon them are their locks, until Allah opens them and relieves them." ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "He became great in my eyes. And this remained in the soul of ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him) until he assumed the caliphate, and he sought help from that young man."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who turned back on their heels﴾, the verse. Qatadah said: It was revealed concerning a people of the Jews who had recognized from the Torah the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ), and guidance had become clear to them in this way. But when they came into contact with his affair, they envied him and turned back from that measure of guidance. Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) and others said: It was revealed concerning hypocrites who had embraced Islam, then their hearts became hypocritical. The verse encompasses everyone who enters within the scope of its wording until the end of time.

The word ﴿سَوَّلَ﴾ (sawwala) means: he made their desires and wishes appear attractive to them. Abu al-Fath related from Abu ʿAli that it means: he lowered them (dallāhum), derived from al-sawal, which is slackness and dangling. The majority of the reciters read ﴿وَأمْلى لَهُمْ﴾ (wa-amlā lahum, "and He prolonged for them"), while Ibn Kathir, Shibl, and Ibn Musarrif read ﴿أمْلى﴾ with imāla (vowel inclination). As for the agent of ﴿أمْلى﴾ here, al-Hasan said: it is Satan, who made his false promise of lasting life like granting respite. This is because imlāʾ is granting continuance for a period of time (milāwah min al-dahr). It is said: milāwah, mulāwah, and malāwah, with the mīm vowelled with ḍamma, fatḥa, or kasra, and it is a portion of time. From this comes al-malawān, which are the night and the day. So when Satan grants respite, it is a respite that has no soundness except through their false hope.

It is also possible that the agent of ﴿أمْلى﴾ is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, as if He, exalted is He, said: Satan made their deeds appear attractive to them, and Allah granted them respite. The true reality of granting respite lies only in the hand of Allah, exalted is He, and this is the more preponderant view.

Al-Aʿraj, Mujahid, al-Jahdari, and al-Aʿmash read ﴿وَأُمْلِي لَهُمْ﴾ (wa-umlī lahum) with a ḍamma on the hamza, a kasra on the lām, and the first-person yāʾ pronounced without elision (irsāl). al-Khifaf related it from Abu ʿAmr. This reading admits as its agent the same range of possibilities as the first reading.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is because they said﴾, the verse. It has been said: it was revealed concerning the Children of Israel mentioned earlier in the exegesis of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who turned back﴾. It is also related that a group from Qurayzah and al-Nadir used to count on the hypocrites, regarding the affair of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and opposition to him, for support and assistance. So that is their saying: ﴿We will obey you in part of the matter.﴾

The majority of reciters read ﴿أسْرارَهُمْ﴾ (asrārahum, "their secrets") with a fatḥa on the hamza, as the plural of sirr, because their secrets were many. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from ʿAsim read ﴿إسْرارَهُمْ﴾ (isrārahum) with a kasra on the hamza. This is the reading of Ibn Waththab, Talhah, al-Aʿmash, and ʿIsa, and it is the verbal noun of the generic noun.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So how will it be when the angels take them in death﴾, the verse. It is possible that they are being threatened with it, and it has two meanings. One is: this is their dread and their panic at the imposition of fighting and the clash with enemies, so how will their terror and panic be when the angels take them in death? Here "they" refers to the Angel of Death and those who act under his direction, and the pronoun in ﴿يَضْرِبُونَ﴾ (yaḍribūna, "they strike") refers to the angels who take them in death. This view is weak.

﴿What angered Allah﴾ is disbelief. And ﴿الرِضْوانُ﴾ (al-riḍwān, "the pleasure") here means the Law and the truth that leads to the pleasure of Allah. The discussion of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so He caused their deeds to be worthless﴾ has already been presented. Al-Aʿmash read: ﴿فَكَيْفَ إذا تَوَفّاهُمُ المَلائِكَةُ﴾ (fa-kayfa idhā tawaffāhumu al-malāʾikah).

This verse is a rebuke to the hypocrites and an exposure of them. His saying, the Exalted, ﴿Or do [they] think﴾, is a rhetorical question, and it is the disjunctive "am" (am al-munqati'a). The explanation of "disease of the heart" has already preceded. His saying, the Exalted, ﴿that Allah will not bring out their malice﴾ means: He will reveal it from its place within their souls. "Al-dhaghn" is rancor.

His saying, the Exalted, ﴿And if We willed, We would show them to you﴾ is an approximation regarding their fame, but He, the Exalted, never specified them by name or by complete identification, out of forbearance toward them and their relatives, even though they had been recognized by the tone of their speech. They were at different levels of notoriety, such as 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy and al-Jadd ibn Qays and others below them in fame. "Al-sima" is the sign which He, the Exalted, would have placed upon them had He willed a complete identification of them. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak said: Allah, the Exalted, did identify them in Surat Bara'a in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And do not pray over any of them who has died, ever﴾ [al-Tawba: 84], and in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Say, "You will never go out with me, ever, and you will never fight an enemy with me"﴾ [al-Tawba: 83]. The greatest of what is narrated regarding their notoriety is that the Prophet ﷺ once gave an order and a group of them was expelled from the mosque, as if he had marked them with this; but they persisted in disavowing that and held fast to "There is no god but Allah," so their blood was protected.

It is narrated from Hudhayfa something that implies that the Prophet ﷺ identified them to him, or some of them, and he had a discussion on this with ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with both of them.

Then He, the Exalted, informed that He would recognize them by the tone of their speech, and its meaning is: in the direction of the speech, its manner and its intent. This is like when a person tells you his belief, and you understand from the breaks in his speech, his bearing, and the circumstances of his affair that he is contrary to what he says. This is the meaning of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿in the tone of speech﴾. From this meaning is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Perhaps some of you is more eloquent (alhan) in his argument than another," the hadith, meaning: he takes it in the directions of speech. This tone may be mutually understood: a person says a statement which the listeners understand one meaning from, and the one who agreed with the speaker understands another meaning. "The best speech is that which is tonal (lahn)"

That is: what your companion understands from you while it remains hidden from others. So Allah, the Exalted, informed His Prophet ﷺ that their damning statements, which are contrary to their creed, would become clear to him, and he would identify them by them. Whoever holds that allusion amounts to slander takes this verse as evidence. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And Allah knows your deeds﴾ is addressed to all, believers and disbelievers alike.

When al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad recited this verse he would weep and say: "O Allah, do not test us, for if You test us You will expose us and tear away our veils." His saying, the Exalted: ﴿until We know those among you who strive and the patient﴾ means: until We know them as strivers whose striving has come into existence and whose acquisition, upon which their reward depends, has become manifest. Allah, blessed and exalted, has eternal, pre-existent knowledge of the strivers, but the meaning is what we have mentioned.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and they averted﴾ may mean: they averted others, and it may be intransitive in meaning, i.e., they averted themselves. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and opposed the Messenger﴾ means: they opposed him, so they were on one side while he ﷺ was on the other. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿after guidance has become clear to them﴾: one group said it was revealed concerning a people of the Children of Israel who did these deeds after they had recognized the matter of Muhammad ﷺ from the Torah.
